rv.q: But it is supremely elegant manipulation, magnificently staged and performed.

The real surprise is that this 'Driving Miss Daisy' works as well as it does, and the reason why is that Ms. Tandy and Mr. Freeman have grown into their roles in ways that make their stage performances richer and more touching than what they did on screen.
The production, directed by David Esbjornson, brings a welcome intimacy to the material, allowing the chemistry between Redgrave and Jones to bloom naturally.
Granted, you often wish the show bared more teeth instead of settling into comfortable, sepia-toned banter.
Still, despite any quibbles, it remains a pleasure to watch these two old pros at work, and Gaines, as usual, is an absolute delight, more than keeping up with his older co-stars.
Even “Driving Miss Daisy,” which opened on Monday night at the Golden Theater.
With three great actors -- Vanessa Redgrave, James Earl Jones and Boyd Gaines -- at their apogee, the enchanting revival of “Driving Miss Daisy” is the best theater can be.
So it shouldn't surprise that Jones' and Redgrave's performances here — by turns funny, tender, adorable and heartbreaking — rank with their best, most revelatory work.
'Daisy' finally makes it to theater's promised land with a dream team that's bound to strike fans as 'the second coming.'
Jones provides a congenial counterpart with an undercurrent of pain.

What unbalances David Esbjornson's sensitively shaped production is, improbably, Redgrave: Her painstakingly detailed quietude and delicacy as Daisy, carefully underplayed to fit what's probably a quite valid concept of the era's notion of ladylike gentility, put the character in a softer focus, reducing her power.
Even worse, there's no apparent bond between these supposed best friends.
So it's with tremendous regret and disappointment that I have to report that this 'Daisy' never fully blooms.
Jones gives a performance that I'd classify as one of the ten or so best I've ever seen in the theatre.

A 'little play' in that its emotions are understated and its brief scenes are mostly everyday situations, 'Driving Miss Daisy' could easily be overwhelmed by actors of such magnificence as Redgrave and Jones, but they unerringly provide honest and nicely-detailed performances that befit the modest story.
